title: Washington Supreme Court Order No. 25700-B-721 — Adoption of a Pilot Project to Test Entity Regulation (5 December 2024)
author: Washington Supreme Court

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The order does not address AI’s jagged capabilities, task selection, verification, or legal-work redesign directly. It provides an analogous adaptive governance model—time-limited authorization, ongoing oversight, and adjustable safeguards—but this is insufficient to establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.

kp.k: Existing ownership restrictions impede testing alternative legal-service entities
kp.d: The Court identifies Washington statutes and professional rules, including Washington RPC 5.4 and LLLT RPC 5.4, as generally restricting legal-service entities to ownership, operation and fee-sharing by authorized practitioners. It acknowledges their public-protection purposes while finding that they obstruct exploration and data-driven testing of entity regulation. This is the Court's regulatory rationale, not a finding that alternative entities improve services.
qs: These rules and statutes generally prohibit the practice of law and provision of legal services by entities unless the entity providing those legal services is owned and operated by, and fees are shared only among, those individuals authorized to practice law;
while serving important public protection purposes, these court rules and statutes serve as barriers to the exploration, and data-driven testing, of legal regulatory reforms

kp.k: Technology motivates experimentation, but benefits remain unproven
kp.d: The WSBA operational page describes online companies and innovative business models as already supplying legal services and predicts their expansion. It frames the pilot as a means of understanding emerging technologies' opportunities and threats for safety, quality and access. The document does not report AI-specific performance or labor-market findings.
qs: Online companies and innovative business models are already delivering legal services to the public and will undoubtedly expand in prevalence and sophistication in the coming years.

Recognizing the profound implications of these changes and to better understand the opportunities and threats presented by emerging technologies — in terms of safety, quality, and access to legal help for Washingtonians — the Washington Supreme Court, the WSBA, and Practice of Law Board (POLB) will operate a pilot test of entity regulation.

kp.k: Pilot permits limited experimentation with nonlawyer-operated entities
kp.d: The 5 December 2024 order directs a collaborative pilot to test reforming activities prohibited by RCW 2.48.180, Washington RPC 5.4 and LLLT RPC 5.4. The WSBA explains that innovative entities, including those operated by people not licensed to practice law, may apply for timebound, limited exemptions. Authorization remains participant-specific and subject to Court orders, rather than constituting permanent market-wide deregulation.
qs: For the first time, entities with innovative business models (including those operated by individuals not licensed to practice law) can apply to offer legal services under timebound, limited exemptions from the otherwise applicable rules governing the practice of law.
For each participant, the Board shall recommend a timebound authorization to practice law that includes appropriate limitations and conditions on that authorization.

kp.k: Applicants must test explicit reform and accessibility hypotheses
kp.d: The pilot uses the Practice of Law Board's Framework for Data-Driven Legal Regulatory Reform. Each applicant must specify a hypothesis connecting proposed regulatory reform to legal-service accessibility in Washington and propose a study to test it. Its primary purpose is evidence collection for regulation of entities undertaking legal and law-related activities; a secondary purpose is assessing the Framework itself.
qs: Each beta-test applicant shall propose (1) a specific hypothesis relating to (a) reforming one or more regulatory rules governing entities practicing law and, if applicable, other related rules and (b) that reform’s impact on the accessibility of legal services in Washington and (2) a study to test that reform.
Secondarily, the purpose of the pilot project is to assess the effectiveness of the Framework, generally, in testing legal regulatory reforms.

kp.k: Access gains must be assessed alongside consumer risks
kp.d: The Court frames increased access to affordable, reliable services as a question for the pilot, alongside consumer harm, regulatory challenges and other obstacles to reform. Its definition of access to justice includes low- and moderate-income Washingtonians and others facing barriers to legal services. These are intended evaluation questions, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: determining whether entity regulation will increase access to justice
by enhancing access to affordable and reliable legal and law-related services consistent with protection of the public
create risks of consumer harm, regulatory challenges, or other risks that would serve as barriers to implementing reform;

For purposes of this Order, “access to justice” means increasing the accessibility of quality legal services to all persons, including low- and moderate-income Washingtonians, and others who experience barriers in accessing legal services.

kp.k: Entity accountability requires compliance officers and continuing oversight
kp.d: Each applicant must designate an authorized practitioner or another suitable person within the entity as compliance officer, responsible for compliance, data reporting and liaison. WSBA and Board oversight addresses authorizing orders and applicable ethics rules. Exemptions do not generally displace business-law obligations, and monitoring or complaints can result in additional protections or removal from the pilot.
qs: Each applicant must identify a person authorized to practice law or other suitable person within the entity to act as a compliance officer

Except for those activities specifically excepted in any authorizing order or law, applicants participating in the pilot project must comply with all other statutes and regulations related to incorporation and conducting business operations in the state of Washington.
The WSBA shall develop complaint procedures for the public to report an alleged violation by an entity or its staff of an authorizing order or an applicable rule of ethics.
up to and including removal from the pilot project.

kp.k: Longitudinal reporting supports reform decisions while protecting confidential information
kp.d: The order requires an entity-specific reporting schedule lasting no more than seven years, covering service provision, authorization compliance and ethics. WSBA must analyze reports and protect confidential client information and trade secrets. WSBA and the Board must report to the Court at least quarterly on operation, participant monitoring and evaluation, aggregate data and findings.
qs: The WSBA shall develop a reporting process and schedule for each entity for a period of time not to exceed seven years.
Entities shall report data and information regarding their provision of legal services, their compliance with their authorizing orders, and their adherence to the rules of ethics.
The WSBA shall securely maintain and safeguard against the unauthorized disclosure of confidential client information or trade secrets collected through reports or by other means.
The WSBA and the Board shall report to the Court at least quarterly

kp.k: Permanent reform remains contingent on pilot evidence
kp.d: The pilot may conclude once sufficient information exists and must end 10 years after the first entity receives Court authorization unless extended. That clock is not tied to the order's issuance or application opening. At conclusion, WSBA and the Board must recommend whether participants should continue, whether additional entity regulation should be implemented or whether testing should continue; continued authorization is not automatic.
qs: In any event, the pilot project shall end 10 years after the date that the first entity is granted authority by the Court to participate in the pilot project, unless extended by the Court.

the Board and the WSBA will make specific, data-driven recommendations to the Court regarding whether to implement any additional entity regulation or to continue testing the concept using the Framework.
The pilot test is the beginning of a process, not the end; the goal is to learn more and make transparent, data-driven decisions before any permanent regulatory reform is put in place.

kp.k: Operational update establishes application availability, not demonstrated outcomes
kp.d: The supplied WSBA page, labeled updated Jan. 9, 2026 and captured 2026-08-16, states that the application portal is open. Its timeline records development beginning in April 2025 and implementation preparations in October 2025 following the December 2024 order. The supplied content reports no participant results or measured effects on access, affordability or quality.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The WSBA predicts expansion of technology-enabled legal services and innovative business models; neither source makes an explicit AI-specific claim.
pts.d: The WSBA operational page states that technology is transforming the legal landscape, that online companies and innovative business models already deliver legal services, and that they will become more prevalent and sophisticated. It presents emerging technologies as creating both opportunities and threats for safety, quality, and access to legal help. Separately, the Washington Supreme Court determines that existing ownership, operation, and fee-sharing restrictions impede testing entity-based legal services. The Court authorizes a pilot to investigate whether entity regulation improves access to affordable, reliable services and creates consumer or regulatory risks. Those potential outcomes are research questions, not findings or promises of AI-driven improvements. The pilot is broader than AI or legal-tech software provision.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The technology-growth prediction is unquantified; the order supplies legal authority and a prospective evidence-collection framework, not outcome evidence.
pts.d: The WSBA offers no named company examples, market data, AI benchmarks, or measured service outcomes for its prediction. The Court grounds its regulatory action in Washington rules and statutes and the Practice of Law Board’s Framework for Data-Driven Legal Regulatory Reform. Applicants must propose hypotheses and studies, and participants must report service and compliance data for analysis. These requirements describe how future evidence will be generated; the supplied document reports no pilot findings establishing improved access, lower costs, reliability, or harm.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Technology-enabled services are described as already operating and expanding in the coming years; regulatory change is conditional and experimental.
pts.d: The WSBA page, marked updated January 9, 2026, gives no precise horizon for its growth prediction beyond 'the coming years.' The December 5, 2024 order establishes a pilot rather than permanent liberalization. Participation requires individual Court authorization with limits and conditions, compliance oversight, and potentially removal. Entity reporting schedules may run for no more than seven years. The pilot ends when sufficient information is available and, unless extended, no later than ten years after the first entity is authorized—not ten years after the order. Permanent reform and continued participant authorization remain subject to later decisions. The page reports that applications are open but supplies no first-authorization date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are Washington legal-service consumers, prospective entity providers including nonlawyer-operated businesses, and the bodies responsible for regulation.
pts.d: Consumers could gain access to affordable, reliable legal help, but possible consumer harm is expressly part of the inquiry. The order specifically includes low- and moderate-income Washingtonians and others facing access barriers. Innovative entities, including those operated by people not licensed to practice law, can seek limited permission to deliver legal services; this is not blanket authorization for all technology vendors. Participants must appoint compliance officers and undergo reporting and oversight. The WSBA, Practice of Law Board, and Court administer, monitor, and decide the future of the experiment. The sources make no concrete predictions about lawyer employment, staffing, billing models, or AI substitution for lawyers.
